No file of your own to hand? Use the Vahedi lab’s sample_sheet_messy.csv, a simulated RNA-seq submission sheet with known problems. (Their afternoon has an exercise that cleans this sheet. Here you’re writing a skill that checks sheets like it and fixes nothing.) Or extend deseq2-triage with a trap from your own lab’s pipeline.
To use the fallback, once you’ve made the skill folder and started a session on it (step 2), ask the agent to fetch the exact file rather than retype it:
Download this file into this folder, saving it byte for byte (curl on macOS,
Invoke-WebRequest on Windows), not by retyping it:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/main/track-a/data/sample_sheet_messy.csv
Then tell me how many rows and columns it has.






ImportantPrivacy: what you show the agent leaves your computer



Anything the agent reads is sent to the model. Use a file you’d be allowed to email to a collaborator: no patient data, nothing identifiable, and nothing unpublished that your lab’s rules keep in-house. For a sensitive file type, describe it in words and make a small fake example.




4.4.2 2. Have the agent interview you
Make a folder called skill inside Documents/agents-workshop/, put a copy of your example file in it (or fetch the fallback, above), and start a new session on that folder, as in Setup. Then paste this, filling in the angle brackets:
I want you to write a skill (a SKILL.md in the Agent Skills format) that checks
<a kind of file, e.g. "the sample sheets we send to our sequencing core"> before
anyone uses it. There's an example in this folder: <file name>.

Don't write anything yet. First interview me, one question at a time, about:
- where these files come from, and what a good one looks like;
- the problems I've actually seen in them, and which would lead to a wrong result;
- anything that can't be checked from the file alone and must be asked of a person;
- what the skill must never do (for example, change the file);
- the words I'd use when asking for this check.

Then show me a draft. The skill must report problems, not fix them, and must say
plainly when something can't be checked from the file. Save it to
.claude/skills/<short-name>/SKILL.md in this folder only when I say it's right.
Answer from experience. The most useful answers are specific: not “check the dates” but “we’ve had three date formats in one sheet, and 3/2/26 means 3 February to our UK collaborators”.


4.4.3 3. Read the draft before you accept it
It’s short; read all of it. Check that:

the description says what it does, then when to use it, in your words;
every trap you mentioned is there, with the reason it matters;
there’s a “do not” for each helpful-looking move you don’t want (fixing the file, filling in missing values, carrying on to an analysis);
the report has a fixed shape, with what stops you first;
it doesn’t claim to check something it can’t. Ask the agent: “Which of these checks could give a wrong answer, and how would I know?”

Ask for changes in plain language. Then let it save the file.


4.4.4 4. Test it on a file where you know the answer
Testing is your job, not the agent’s. It needs two files.

A good file. A real one you’ve already checked by hand. The skill should report little or nothing, and nothing false.
A bad file. Copy the good one and break it yourself: add a duplicate row, delete a value, change one date format, misspell a sample name. Write down what you broke before you run the check. Then you know exactly what it should find.

Run each in a new session, so the agent that wrote the skill can’t answer from memory, with a prompt that doesn’t name the skill:
I've just been sent <file name>. Is it OK to use?
Compare what it reports with your list. Anything missed means the instructions need work. Anything it invented is worse: tell the agent exactly what it claimed, and ask it to change the skill so that can’t happen again.


4.4.5 5. Test the description
Now test the part that decides whether the skill ever runs. Write three requests that should load it and three neighbouring ones that shouldn’t. Use how you’d really ask, not how you’d describe the skill.










Should load it
Should not load it




“Can you look over this sample sheet?”
“Make me a blank sample sheet template”


“Is this ready to send to the core?”
“What does the core charge per lane?”


“Anything wrong with tconv_batch2.csv?”
“Plot the harvest dates in this sheet”





Table 4.5: An example should/shouldn’t pair for a sample-sheet checker.



Try each in a new session. If you can’t tell from the transcript whether the skill was used, ask “Did you use a skill for that?”. When a phrasing you’d genuinely use doesn’t load it, tell the agent the phrase and ask it to revise the description, then test again. The usual failure is a skill that loads too rarely, not too often, so lean towards a description with more of your everyday words in it.






TipIf it never loads at all



Ask “What skills are available?”. If yours isn’t listed, the folder is in the wrong place, or the header between the --- lines is malformed. Ask the agent to check both. You can always run a skill directly by typing / and its name.

title: 4  Write a skill
text:
4.5 What to notice

You wrote almost none of it, and it still encodes exactly what you know. The value was in your answers and your tests, not the typing.
The “do not” lines did real work. Without them, a checking skill drifts into a fixing skill, and a fixed file hides the problem you most needed to see.
The agent can’t verify its own skill. It can check that the file is well formed. Only a file where you know the answer tells you whether the checks are right.
The description is an interface. It failed silently or it worked; there was no error message either way.

4.6 Check yourself






TipYou’re done when




Your skill is at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md in your project folder.
On your good file, it reported nothing false.
On your broken file, it found everything you planted, or you’ve changed it so it does.
It loaded for a phrasing that isn’t copied from its description, and didn’t load for a neighbouring request.
You’ve added a ledger entry (Chapter 2) saying what you tested it on and what it missed.

text:
4.7 Going further

Real examples. Anthropic’s life-sciences repository publishes skills for scientific work. Read single-cell-rna-qc: a SKILL.md that runs Python scripts from scripts/ and reads scverse QC guidance from references/ only when needed. It’s the same format you just used, grown larger.
Share it with your lab. A skill in a project’s .claude/skills/ travels with the project. Put it in a shared lab folder or repository (Chapter 7), and every trainee who starts there gets your checks without having to know they exist.
Measure it. The skill-creator plugin for Claude Code runs a skill against test prompts with and without it, and suggests description changes. See “Evaluate and iterate on a skill” in the skills documentation (“Extend Claude with Skills,” n.d.).
Connect it to data. Skills tell an agent how; MCP servers (Chapter 5) give it access to databases it can’t otherwise reach. The two combine.

title: 5  Connect to a database (MCP)
text:
5.1 What you’ll learn
Ask an agent for “recent papers on TCF-1 and chromatin in T cells” and it will answer from memory. That memory is large, and it is often right, but it is frozen at the date the model was trained, and it has no way to tell a paper it read from a paper that merely sounds plausible. Language models are known to invent references: in one study, 18% of the citations GPT-4 produced for short literature reviews did not exist, and a quarter of the real ones had substantive errors (Walters and Wilder 2023). Newer models are better at saying “I don’t know”, but “better” is not a standard you can cite.
The fix is not a cleverer prompt. It is to let the agent ask the system of record: search PubMed itself, get back real PMIDs, and show you where each fact came from. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how that connection is made (“What Is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?” n.d./). An MCP server sits in front of a database or service and offers the agent a handful of tools, such as “search articles” or “get article metadata”. The agent decides when to call them and what to ask. You add the server once, and from then on it is part of what the agent can do.
In Chapter 4 you gave the agent instructions: how your lab triages a results table. A skill tells the agent how. An MCP server tells it what is there now. This chapter connects one server, PubMed, which needs no account, and then does the thing that matters most: checks what came back.

title: 5  Connect to a database (MCP)
text:
What an MCP server is, and how it differs from a skill.
How to connect the PubMed server, three ways: by asking the agent, from the command line, or as a plugin from Anthropic’s life-sciences marketplace.
How to compare an answer from memory with an answer from a live database.
How to check retrieved results by hand, and why retrieval is not the same as truth.
What an MCP server can see, and which servers to trust.

title: 5  Connect to a database (MCP)
text:
5.2 How an MCP connection works
An MCP server is a small program, usually run by whoever owns the data, that speaks one agreed protocol. When your agent starts, it asks each configured server “what tools do you have?” and gets back a list with names, descriptions and inputs. From then on, whenever a question needs one of those tools, the agent calls it, reads the result and carries on (Figure 5.1).

    Server->>PubMed: search

    Server-->>Agent: PMIDs
    Agent->>Server: get_article_metadata([PMIDs])
    Server-->>Agent: titles, authors, journals
    Agent-->>You: three papers, with PMIDs and sources




Figure 5.1: One question, answered through the PubMed MCP server. The agent chooses the tools and the search terms; the server turns each call into a query against PubMed and returns the records.







Protocol: an agreed way for two programs to talk. Because MCP is shared, the same PubMed server works with Claude Code, Claude’s desktop app, Google Antigravity, Codex and Copilot. Only the place you configure it differs.
Two things follow from this picture. First, the agent writes the query. You asked in plain English; the agent turned that into search terms, and a search can match the wrong organism, the wrong assay or the wrong TCF (there are several). Second, the server sees your question, or at least the parts of it the agent sends. Both come back later in this chapter.

5.2.1 Anthropic’s life-sciences servers
Anthropic keeps a list of MCP servers and skills for life sciences in a public GitHub repository, packaged as Claude Code plugins in a marketplace (Anthropic 2026). A plugin is a bundle; a marketplace is a list of plugins you can install by name. The servers themselves are run by the data providers, not by Anthropic. PubMed, which this chapter uses, is one of them; “Going further” lists some of the others (Table 5.5).
PubMed is not in the official Anthropic marketplace that Claude Code sets up for you. To install it as a plugin you add the life-sciences marketplace first. The simpler route, which works in every tool, is to give the agent the server’s address directly.

T cells. For each give the first author, year, journal, title and PMID. Say where each
fact came from.
The bare agent was careful. It said it had no way to look anything up, gave three papers from memory, and left the PMIDs blank, “because I don’t remember them reliably, and a made-up PMID is worse than a blank”. All three papers turned out to be real. But you could not have known that from the answer, and without PMIDs you had to do the searching yourself.
Then we connected PubMed in the second folder, using the .mcp.json file you’ll write in a moment, and asked again. This time the agent searched PubMed twice (search_articles) and fetched the records it found (get_article_metadata), and came back in about 30 seconds with Table 5.2.

Just as useful was what it said about its own work:

It picked papers 1 and 3 from their titles alone, and said so: “I didn’t read its abstract.”
Paper 2 did not come up in its broad search. It remembered the paper, searched for it by name, and took every detail from the PubMed record. It said that too.
Paper 3 is about chromatin accessibility, not 3D structure, which it flagged as a partial fit.

Then we checked. We looked up all three PMIDs directly in PubMed, independently of the agent: every title, first author, journal and year matched. We also checked the paper the bare agent had remembered but the connected one did not use (Shan 2021, Nat Commun); it is real too (Shan et al. 2021).

Shan, Qiang, Xiang Li, Xia Chen, et al. 2021. “Tcf1 and Lef1 Provide Constant Supervision to mature CD8.” Nature Communications 12 (1): 5863. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26159-1.
So memory did not fail here, and that is the honest result. What changed is that the answer became checkable: every claim came with an identifier and a stated source, and the agent separated what it had read from what it had inferred from a title.






NoteIs the second paper really about 3D genome structure?



The agent read that abstract and quoted it: Tcf1 and CTCF together “promote chromatin interactions and form highly connected, dynamic interaction hubs”. That is a claim about the paper, not a PMID, and checking it means reading the abstract yourself. That is the part of the check that no tool does for you.

title: 5  Connect to a database (MCP)
text:
5.4 Your turn
You’ll need about 20 minutes. Inside your agents-workshop folder in Documents (from Setup), make a new folder called mcp, and start a new session on it. Ask “what folder are you in?” to be sure. Everything in this chapter happens in agents-workshop/mcp, and its LEDGER.md lives there too (Chapter 2).






ImportantPrivacy: what leaves your machine



Every tool call sends the agent’s query to the server’s operator. For PubMed that means your search terms: a topic, gene names, a disease. That is usually fine. Don’t put anything in a query you wouldn’t type into the PubMed website: no patient details, and nothing about unpublished work you’ve been asked to keep quiet.



5.4.1 1. Ask first, without a connection
Pick a topic you know well enough to judge an answer: your own field, a method you use, a gene you study. Start a new session and ask:
Find three recent papers on <your topic>. For each give the first author, year,
journal, title and PMID. Say where each fact came from. Don't search the web, and
don't use any PubMed or other database tools.

title: 5  Connect to a database (MCP)
text:
5.5 What to notice

The agent chose the tools and wrote the queries. You never saw PubMed’s search syntax. That’s convenient, and it’s also where silent errors come from: look at the search terms it used (ask it) before trusting that “no papers found” means none exist.
Retrieval is not truth. A real PMID proves the paper exists. It doesn’t prove the paper says what the agent claims, or that it’s the best paper on the topic. The agent in our worked example chose two papers from their titles and said so. Ask yours to do the same.
The good answer showed its sources. Compare how each answer said where its facts came from. That, more than the facts, is what the connection bought.
You added a capability without writing code. Four lines of JSON, and the agent can now search a database it couldn’t reach before.

WarningWhich servers to trust



A server you connect can see every query the agent sends it, and its answers go straight into the agent’s work. Content a server returns can even contain instructions aimed at the agent (a prompt injection), which is why Claude Code’s documentation says to verify you trust each server before connecting it (“Connect Claude Code to Tools via MCP,” n.d.). Plugins are trusted more still: they can run code on your machine.

Install servers from the data’s owner or from a source you trust, such as the NLM, the Open Targets consortium or Anthropic’s own list, not from a random repository.
For servers that need an account, treat the token like a password. Don’t paste it into the chat, and don’t put it in a .mcp.json you’ll share or commit.
Your institution’s rules on data still apply. A connection doesn’t change what you’re allowed to send.

title: 6  Build an app
text:
6.1 What you’ll learn
In Chapter 1 you asked for a web page and got one. That page said things. An app does things: it reads your file, works something out, and shows you an answer. That is where agents are at their most impressive, and where they fail most quietly. Ask for “a page that looks up my genes in a DESeq2 table” and within a few minutes you’ll have one that loads, looks tidy and gives answers. Whether those answers are right is a separate question, and the page won’t tell you. A fold change read the wrong way round, an NA treated as “not significant”, chr10 sorted before chr2: each one produces a page that works perfectly and is wrong.
This morning’s talk put the reason plainly. A one-line request leaves dozens of decisions unmade, and the agent quietly guesses every one. Most guesses are reasonable. All of them being right is the unlikely part. The fix is not a cleverer model or a longer prompt. It’s a specification: a short document that says what the app does, what it doesn’t, what goes in, and how you’ll know it’s right. It records the decisions, so nobody has to guess them.
You won’t write that spec yourself, and you won’t write any code. The agent will interview you, one question at a time, and write the spec from your answers. Then it builds the app from the spec. Your job is the part only you can do: knowing what would actually help in your work, and knowing the right answers for a small test case. This chapter gives you a starter prompt that runs the whole conversation, from “what do you work on?” to a working app in a folder on your laptop.

title: 6  Build an app
text:
What goes in a small, useful spec, and what goes wrong when each part is missing.
Why a test case with answers worked out by hand is the most important part of it.
How to let an agent interview you into a spec, rather than writing one.

text:
6.2 What a spec is
A spec for a small app fits on two pages. It has seven parts (Table 6.1), and each one exists because of a particular way things go wrong.

Table 6.1: The seven parts of a small spec, and what goes wrong without each.



The test case deserves a word of its own. An agent that writes the code and works out the expected answers by running that code has only shown that the code agrees with itself. The answers have to come from somewhere else: from rules written down before any code existed, checked by a person. That’s you. The rule that goes with it is simple: never change the answers to make a test pass. If the code disagrees with an answer you checked, the code is wrong.


Fixture is the programmer’s word for a small test file with known answers. PeakPeek’s is 17 lines long, and every line is there to catch one particular mistake.
The order matters as much as the parts. The conversation goes from your work to your computer to the spec, and only then to code, with you approving the spec before anything is built (Figure 6.1).

title: 6  Build an app
text:
6.3 Worked example: PeakPeek
PeakPeek is a page that tells you what’s in a peak file: how many peaks, how wide, on which chromosomes, and what’s wrong with the file. Its spec is much longer than the one you’ll write, about 440 lines, because it was written to be built by a roomful of people without anyone to ask. But it has the same seven parts. Its reference data are five public ENCODE peak files from mouse thymus (Abascal et al. 2020), with the right answers for each worked out with awk, Python and bedtools, independently of any app. Its fixture is a 17-line BED file with a blank line, a zero-width peak, a start that isn’t a number, and a chr10 placed to catch anyone who sorts chromosome names as text.

Abascal, Federico and, Reyes Acosta, Nicholas J. Addleman, et al. 2020. “Expanded Encyclopaedias of DNA Elements in the Human and Mouse Genomes.” Nature 583 (7818): 699–710. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2493-4.
With a spec that complete, the building was not the slow part. We gave a fresh agent (Claude Opus 5.5) an empty folder, the spec and a single prompt, twice. It built the whole page in 15 minutes the first time and 13 the second, and both pages worked first time, with every test passing (Figure 6.2 shows the finished version).






Figure 6.2: PeakPeek, the finished version, with two ENCODE files loaded by URL: CTCF and H3K4me3. The CTCF card’s numbers (20,220 peaks, median width 344 bp, 6,003,019 bp after merging overlaps) match the answers worked out with bedtools.



What the builds got wrong is more instructive than what they got right. Almost every problem traced back to the spec, not the code:

An undefined word. The spec asked for a count of “overlapping peaks” but never said what counted as overlapping. Two builds chose differently and reported 1,763 and 3,457 for the same CTCF file. Both were reasonable; they couldn’t both be the answer.
A wrong definition, with the right answer. The spec said the CTCF file had one “exact duplicate” line. It has two lines with the same position and different scores. The count of 1 was right; the description was wrong. A build found it.
A rule that contradicted itself. “Accept 1e+03, reject 1.5e2” looks tidy until you notice that 1.5e2 is 150, a perfectly good whole number, and that R writes large numbers exactly this way.
Something that could never work. The first draft had the test page read its answers from a separate file. A page opened by double-clicking isn’t allowed to read other files, so that test could never have passed. The answers moved into a script.

Every fresh build found something. That’s the case for running the check, and for having a spec to fix: the correction goes into one place, and the next build gets it. The finished PeakPeek is public at https://github.com/seandavi/peakpeek, and you can use it at https://seandavi.github.io/peakpeek/.

title: 6  Build an app
section: 6.4 Worked example: the starter prompt, tested
text:
6.4 Worked example: the starter prompt, tested
The prompt you’ll use in a moment was tested before it reached you. We played the part of an attendee: a postdoc studying gene regulation in B cells, with a DESeq2 (Love et al. 2014) results table from the Vahedi lab’s workshop data and a project folder with the kind of AGENTS.md you wrote in Chapter 3. The agent was Claude Code on a Mac. The answers were ours, typed from a script, so your conversation will go differently; that’s the point of it.

Love, Michael I, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders. 2014. “Moderated Estimation of Fold Change and Dispersion for RNA-seq Data with DESeq2.” Genome Biology 15 (12). https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8.
Here is what happened, stage by stage.
The idea. The agent read the project’s README and AGENTS.md, then asked before opening the data. Allowed to look at the first few lines, it checked the fold-change direction against the raw counts itself (Myc: about 600 reads in the knockout, 1,600 in wild type, log2 fold change +1.19, so positive means lower in the knockout, as AGENTS.md said). It then offered three ideas, each built around a mistake the table invites: a gene lookup that states the direction in words, a sanity report for any new table from the core, and an exporter for significant-gene lists. We picked the lookup.
Your computer. Without installing anything, it reported the operating system and versions of R, RStudio, Python, Node and git, then recommended a single web page, on the grounds that it needs nothing new, works on Windows, and keeps the data on the laptop.
The spec. 130 lines, all seven parts. The test case was a seven-gene table: two real genes copied from the file and five made-up ones, each built to test one trap: a padj of NA, a symbol shared by two genes, a padj of exactly 0.05, an Ensembl ID with a version suffix, and an ID that isn’t in the table. It showed its working for each answer and asked us to confirm them. It raised five open decisions, and flagged the one that mattered most: keep the fold change as written in the file, and let the words carry the direction.
The build. Two minutes. Its own test compared the page’s output with our eight approved rows and matched every one. It reported what it had checked, and what it hadn’t: it had not clicked through the page itself, nor tried pasting into slides. So we did: the page, opened in Chrome and given the test file, produced exactly the eight rows (Figure 6.3).






Figure 6.3: The gene lookup built in the test run, given its own seven-gene test table. Five of the genes are made up, each to test one trap: a missing padj, a shared symbol, a padj of exactly 0.05, an ID that isn’t there. The yellow line states the direction of the fold change at all times.



Three things went less well, and the prompt below was changed because of them:

Its test needed Node, a programming tool many attendees won’t have, especially on Windows. The prompt now asks for a test you can run with only what’s on your computer: for a web page, a test.html you double-click. A second run of the revised prompt did exactly that, and its test.html showed 17 of 17 checks passing when we opened it.
It went beyond the spec without asking. It added a second clipboard format so tables paste properly into slides. That was sensible, and it told us, but the prompt had said to ask first. The second run did the same with three small choices, listed them, and asked afterwards. Watch for this: an agent’s idea of “obviously helpful” is still a decision, and decisions belong in the spec.
We rubber-stamped the answers. Our script said “all correct” without checking. We checked afterwards, and they were, but that’s luck, not a method. The second run’s spec had eleven answers, including fold changes like 20.3 = 1.23: easy to check with a calculator, and easy to skip.

In the second run, with the same scripted answers, the agent made a different and arguably better choice: the app refuses to show results until you say which group a positive fold change favours, because getting that backwards is the most likely mistake. It asked before reading more than the first few lines of the real file, and the whole conversation took under seven minutes of the agent’s time, four of them building. Same prompt, same person, different app. Neither is wrong. That’s why the spec exists: it’s where you see the choice and make it yours.

title: 6  Build an app
text:
6.5 Your turn
You’ll need about 30–45 minutes, most of it conversation. The build itself is usually the short part.

6.5.1 1. Make a folder, start a new session
Make a new folder called my-app inside Documents/agents-workshop, next to the folders from earlier chapters. Not inside your project from Chapter 3: the app is a new thing, and it gets its own folder. Start a new session on it, as in Setup (in the Claude desktop app, choose the folder as the session’s project folder), and check with “what folder are you in?”
If you did Chapter 3, have the path to that project folder to hand. The agent will ask.






ImportantPrivacy: your data and the agent



The app itself can keep your data on your laptop: a page opened by double-clicking reads files without sending them anywhere. The conversation doesn’t. Anything the agent reads, including “the first few lines of the data file”, is sent to the model. The morning’s rule applies: nothing identifiable, no patient data, nothing unpublished you aren’t allowed to share. If in doubt, ask the agent to invent a small example in the same format, and try your real file only in the finished app.




6.5.2 2. Paste the starter prompt
I'd like to build a small app with you: one I'd actually use in my work. I don't write
code, and I don't want to start now. Lead me through it in four stages, and don't start
the next stage until I say so. Ask me one question at a time. Look around before you ask
anything you could find out yourself.

Stage 1, the idea. Ask what I work on. If I point you to a project folder, read its
README and AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md) first, and ask before opening anything else there.
Then suggest three small app ideas that would save me time or catch mistakes in my
work. Each should be something I could describe in two sentences and try on one file.
Help me pick one and cut it down to the smallest useful version.

Stage 2, my computer. Without installing anything, find out which operating system I'm
on and whether R, RStudio, Python, Node and git are installed. Tell me what you found.
Then pick the simplest way to build the app that needs nothing new. If in doubt, make
it a web page: one folder, opened by double-clicking index.html, with no server, no
packages and no internet needed to run it. It must work on Windows as well as macOS.

Stage 3, the spec. Write a short SPEC.md in this folder, two pages at most:
- Purpose: who it's for, and the question it answers.
- What it does, as a numbered list.
- What it doesn't do.
- Inputs: formats, with a real example of each.
- A tiny test case: an input small enough to check by eye, and its right answers,
  worked out by hand. Show me the working, and ask me to confirm each answer.
- Open decisions, each with a suggested default.
- Done when: a short checklist I can tick myself.
Then ask me to read it. Write no code until I say "approved".

Stage 4, the build. Build exactly what SPEC.md describes. Save the test case and its
answers as files, with a test I can run myself using only what's on my computer (for a
web page, a test.html I double-click). Never change the answers to make a test pass: if
the code disagrees, fix the code, or stop and tell me. If something needs more than the
spec says, ask me first. Then add an entry to LEDGER.md (start one if there isn't one),
with the headings Asked / Agent did / Checked how / Confidently wrong / Keep, and tell
me how to open the app, what you checked and how, and what you couldn't check.


6.5.3 3. Have the conversation
A few things make it go well.

Answer in your own words. “I get DESeq2 tables from the core and I always forget which way the fold change goes” is a perfect answer. So is “I don’t know, what would you suggest?”
Say “smaller”. The first idea is almost always too big. The smallest useful version is something you could try on one file this afternoon.
Take the suggested defaults for the open decisions the first time through, unless one is plainly wrong for your work. You can change them later; that’s what the spec is for.
Check the test answers yourself. This is the one step you can’t hand over. Work each one out from the rules in the spec, with a calculator if you need one. If you can’t tell whether an answer is right, the rule is unclear: ask for it to be rewritten.
Read the spec before you say “approved”. Two pages. Anything you don’t understand is a question worth asking now.







TipIf it goes wrong




The agent wants to install something. Say no, and ask for a way that needs nothing new. A web page almost always works.
The spec is long. “Cut it to two pages; move anything optional to ‘What it doesn’t do’.”
It stopped halfway through the build. Say “continue”.
A blank page. Open the browser’s console (⌥⌘J on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows, in Chrome or Edge) and paste the red text to the agent.
A test fails. Ask “is the code wrong, or the expected answer?” You checked the answers, so it’s the code, unless you find you made a mistake. If you did, fix the answer in the spec first, deliberately, and say why in the ledger.









NoteOn Windows






Double-clicking index.html opens it in your default browser, usually Edge. That’s fine: Edge and Chrome behave the same here.
File extensions are hidden by default, so index.html may show as index; see



Checking what’s installed: the agent may run commands in PowerShell rather than a Unix shell, and ask permission for each. They only read version numbers; allowing them is safe.
R and RStudio are often installed without being on the command line’s path, so the agent may not find them at first. If you know they’re there, tell it.






6.5.4 4. Try it, then save it
Open the app and run its test first: every answer should match the ones you checked. Then try it on a real file, and on something it should reject. Ask the agent about anything that surprises you.
Chapter 7 carries on with this app, so keep the folder. When you’re happy with it, ask:
Copy everything in this folder except snapshots/ into snapshots/first-build/.






NoteNo idea, or no time?



Build PeakPeek instead. The spec is finished, and one prompt builds it: PeakPeek: a page built in one prompt. Then come back and use the starter prompt on an idea of your own when one arrives.

title: 6  Build an app
text:
6.6 What to notice

The questions found decisions you didn’t know you were making. Which way does the fold change go? Is exactly 0.05 significant? What happens to a gene that isn’t there? Each one would have been a silent guess.
The build was fast; the checking was yours. A few minutes of building sat behind a conversation several times as long. That’s the right proportion.
“What I couldn’t check” is the most useful part of the report. In our test, the agent couldn’t click through its own page. It said so. The page was right, but only because we went and looked.
Did it go beyond the spec? Anything it added unasked is a decision somebody made without you. Put it in the spec, or take it out.

TipYou’re done when




Your folder has a SPEC.md you’ve read, with a test case whose answers you worked out yourself.
The app opens by double-clicking, with nothing installed for it.
Its test passes, and you ran it yourself.

title: 6  Build an app
text:
6.8 Going further

A new session for the build. For anything bigger than this, the Claude Code documentation recommends writing the spec in one session and building from it in a fresh one, which has nothing in its context but the spec (“Best Practices for Claude Code,” n.d.). The spec is the distillate; hand over the distillate, not the conversation.
Build it twice. Give the same spec to two fresh sessions and compare the apps. Wherever they differ, the spec left something open.
A bigger spec. Spec first, then build: peak overlap is a spec at the scale of a real project, and peakwhere is that spec built by agents, with every decision and review on the record.
Keep going with your app. Chapter 7 turns it into a project: a ledger entry for every change, a record of each decision, and a way back when a change goes wrong.




“Best Practices for Claude Code.” n.d. Accessed September 23, 2026. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.1 What you’ll learn
The app you built in Chapter 6 is finished in the sense that it works. If you never open it again, that’s enough. But most useful things get opened again. Next month you’ll want it to read another file format, a colleague will ask why it rounds the way it does, and you’ll ask an agent to make “one small change” that quietly breaks something you checked by hand three weeks ago.
At that point two questions matter, and a chat transcript answers neither. The first is why is it like this? Somebody chose to reject zero-width peaks, or to draw charts without a library, or to treat CSV coordinates as 0-based. If that choice isn’t written down, the next person to touch the code, and the agent most of all, will “fix” it. An agent tidying code can’t tell a deliberate decision from an accident. The second is how do I get back? Agents edit many files quickly and confidently. When a change goes wrong you want to return to the last version that worked, exactly, without remembering what it looked like.
Software projects settled both questions long ago, and the answers are cheap. This chapter adds three habits to the app you already have: the ledger from Chapter 2, for every change; decision records, for the few choices that would be awkward to undo; and git, the undo button, if you have it or can install it. If you can’t, you’ll keep dated copies of the folder instead, and that is fine.
You don’t have to type git commands, or remember them. The agent runs them. Your job is the same as everywhere else in this book: say what you want, and check what happened.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
Why a project you’ll come back to needs a record of what was decided and why, not just what the code does.
How to write a short architecture decision record (ADR), and why “must not” in a file called adr/ works on agents as well as people.
How to have the agent commit each change with a real message, show you the history, and go back when something breaks.
What to do instead if git isn’t available: snapshots.
Where to go next: GitHub, issues and pull requests.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.2 Three records, three questions
Each habit answers a different question, and they don’t replace each other (Table 7.1). The ledger is the story of your work with the agent: what you asked, what it did, how you checked. A decision record is the reason behind one choice, written once and kept. A commit is the exact change to the files, with a way back.

Table 7.1: What each record is for. None is edited to rewrite the past.



A useful rhythm is one loop per change (Figure 7.1). Decide whether it’s a decision worth recording; if so, write the record first, so the agent builds to it. Make the change. Check it. Write the ledger entry. Commit.






flowchart LR
  accDescr: One loop per change. Next change; if awkward to reverse, write an ADR first; make the change; check it; if broken, go back; if it works, ledger entry, then commit or snapshot.
  A[Next change] --> B{Awkward to<br/>reverse?}
  B -- yes --> C[Write an ADR]
  B -- no --> D[Make the change]
  C --> D
  D --> E[Check it:<br/>tests, by eye]

Figure 7.1: One loop per change. The decision record comes first, when there is one, so the agent builds to it. Nothing is committed that hasn’t been checked.






7.2.1 Decision records
An architecture decision record is a short numbered file, one per decision, with three parts: the context that forced a choice, the decision, and its consequences, good and bad. Michael Nygard proposed the format in 2011, for software teams that kept losing the reasons behind their own designs (“Documenting Architecture Decisions” 2011). They live together in a folder called adr/, numbered in order: 0001-…md, 0002-…md.

“Documenting Architecture Decisions.” 2011. November 15. https://www.cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions.
Two rules make them work. First, write only the decisions that would be awkward to reverse, or that someone would be tempted to undo: which coordinate convention a file uses, whether to depend on a library, what counts as a duplicate. “Make the button blue” isn’t one. Second, a decision record is never edited to reverse it. If you change your mind, you write a new record that says it supersedes the old one, and mark the old one “superseded by …”. The history of your thinking stays readable. Fixing a factual slip in the wording is fine, and it’s honest to append a short “Correction” note saying so.


This workshop keeps its own. The day you’re attending changed shape the day before it ran: ADR-0001 set a timetable, and ADR-0007 superseded it. Both are still there.
Decision records turn out to suit agents unusually well. An agent reads a folder before it changes things, and it follows plain, imperative rules. “We generally prefer hand-written charts” reads to an agent as a preference it can weigh against your latest request. “The page must not load anything from the network” reads as a rule. Write the Decision section with must and must not, and add one line to your AGENTS.md (Chapter 3) telling the agent to read adr/ before changing behaviour.


7.2.2 Git, the undo button
git records the state of every file in a folder each time you commit, with a message saying what changed and why. You can list the history, see exactly what changed between any two points, and put the folder back the way it was. It has a reputation for being hard, and typing it by hand can be. But you won’t be typing it: the agent knows git thoroughly, and you ask in plain words.
Four ideas are enough for this chapter:











Idea
What it means
Ask the agent




Commit

“Commit this, with a message that says what and why.”


History
The list of commits
“Show me the history, one line per commit.”

“What’s changed since the last commit?”


Revert
Undo a commit by adding a new one that reverses it
“Revert the last commit.”





Table 7.2: Enough git for this chapter.



A fifth, branch, is a separate line of history for an experiment. If the experiment works, you merge it back; if not, you switch back and delete it, and nothing else was touched.


Claude Code also keeps its own checkpoints: in the terminal, /rewind (or pressing Esc twice) can undo its file edits within a session. But it doesn’t undo changes made by commands the agent ran, and the checkpoints expire, by default after about 30 days (“Checkpointing,” n.d.). git covers everything, and keeps it.

“Checkpointing.” n.d. Accessed September 23, 2026. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing.
A commit stays on your computer. Nothing goes anywhere unless you later choose to put the folder on GitHub (see “Going further”). Even so, git keeps everything you ever committed, so a file you commit and then delete is still in the history. Decide before your first commit what should never be in the folder’s history: data you couldn’t share, passwords, keys.


7.2.3 No git? Snapshots
Some laptops won’t let you install anything, and some people would rather not today. Then ignore git entirely. Before each change, ask the agent: “Copy everything in this folder except snapshots/ into snapshots//”, with a short name for what’s about to change. Going back means copying a snapshot back. You lose the tidy history and the exact diffs, but you keep the part that matters most, which is a way back to something that worked. The ledger and the decision records work exactly the same without git.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.3 Worked example
PeakPeek is a small browser page that summarises a peak file: widths, chromosomes, duplicates, overlaps. It’s the same app as the fallback in Chapter 6, built the long way by several agents in one afternoon, with Sean as the maintainer (an agent did most of the maintaining on his behalf, and the records say so). Its folder holds a specification, eleven decision records, a four-entry ledger and fifteen commits (Figure 7.2). It’s small enough to read in ten minutes, and every record in it is real.






Figure 7.2: PeakPeek’s history on GitHub. Each commit is one checked piece of work, and the messages say what changed and why.



A decision record. The specification left eleven questions open, and each got an ADR (Figure 7.3). Here is 0009, in full (rewrapped to fit):
# 0009 — Hand-written SVG or a charting library

**Status:** accepted
**Deciders:** orchestrating agent, acting for Sean Davis
(not yet reviewed by him). SPEC.md §6 Q9, suggested default taken.

## Context

A library means a CDN (network, and a third party sees the page
load) or a copy in the folder (and its licence).

## Decision

Hand-written SVG.

## Consequences

About 60 lines per chart; no dependencies at all.
Three short sentences. Without them, an agent asked to “make the histogram nicer” might well reach for a charting library, and the page would quietly start loading code from someone else’s server.






Figure 7.3: PeakPeek’s adr/ folder: one file per decision, an index, and a template to copy.



A change that touched all three records. After the first build, a second agent built the same app independently from the same spec, as a test of the spec. Wherever the two builds disagreed, the spec hadn’t said something. One disagreement showed that ADR-0003 was wrong about a fact: the CTCF file’s “exact duplicate line” was really two peaks with the same coordinates and different scores. The decision (count duplicates and flag them) still stood, so the record wasn’t rewritten. It got a “Correction” note appended. The commit that made the fix, 35c2f42, changed three files together: the spec, the ADR’s correction, and ledger entry 4, which reads in part:

Confidently wrong — Orchestrator: SPEC §2 said CTCF has “an exact duplicate line”. It has a duplicate peak: same coordinates, different scores. […] ADR-0003 has a correction note.
Keep — A second independent build is a cheap test of a spec: every place the two disagree is a sentence the spec didn’t write.

A mistake the records caught. Ledger entry 2 records that, while five agents were writing code in the same folder, the orchestrating agent committed a spec change with a command that commits every changed file. It swept three agents’ half-finished code into the commit. One of the other agents noticed, and the commit was redone with the spec alone. The lesson went into the ledger’s “Keep” field. You probably won’t run five agents at once, but the general point holds: look at what a commit includes before trusting it, which is why the prompts below ask the agent to show you.
What we checked for this section: the commit list, the ADR folder and the files quoted above, read directly from the repository on 23 September 2026. We didn’t re-run PeakPeek’s tests for this chapter; its ledger records how they were checked.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.4 Your turn
You need the folder from Chapter 6, Documents/agents-workshop/my-app, with your app in it and its LEDGER.md. No app? Use the PeakPeek exercise from Chapter 6 as your starting point, or any small folder you care about. Start a new session in that folder, and ask “What folder are you in?” before anything else.
Allow 30–40 minutes. There are three steps: set up, two changes, and one deliberate mistake. With git, your history will end up looking something like Figure 7.4.

  commit id: "Starting point"
  commit id: "ADR-0001 + change 1" tag: "Ledger 1"
  commit id: "Change 2" tag: "Ledger 2"
  branch try-idea
  commit id: "Experiment"
  checkout main
  commit id: "Deliberate mistake"
  commit id: "Revert mistake" tag: "Ledger 3"




Figure 7.4: Where this chapter’s activity leaves you: a starting point, two changes (one with a decision record), a mistake and its revert, each with a ledger entry. The optional experiment branch is never merged here, so main never sees it.











WarningBefore your first commit



git keeps everything you ever commit. If the folder holds data you couldn’t share, anything identifiable, or any password or key, move it out, or have it listed in .gitignore so git never records it, before the first commit. Snapshots keep copies too: the same care applies.



7.4.1 1. Set up
First, find out whether you have git. Paste this:
Is git installed on this computer? Just check, and tell me the version
if so. Don't install anything yet. If it isn't installed, tell me the
simplest way to install it on my operating system, and wait for me.

macOS: typing git in Terminal usually offers to install Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include git. Accept, and wait a few minutes. The agent may suggest xcode-select --install, which does the same.
Windows: install Git for Windows, or, in PowerShell, winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget. Then start a new agent session so it can find git.
Can’t install it (a managed laptop, or no time): skip every git step below and use the snapshot prompts instead. You lose nothing that matters for this chapter.







NoteOn Windows





After installing Git for Windows, restart the Claude desktop app or your terminal before asking again. The installer’s defaults are fine. Claude Code on Windows uses git’s bundled Git Bash to run commands when it’s installed, and PowerShell when it isn’t (“Advanced Setup,” n.d.); either works for this chapter. Folder paths will look like snapshots\start.
OneDrive and git can clash. If your Documents folder is synced to OneDrive, OneDrive may lock or re-sync files inside the hidden .git folder while git is writing them, and the repository can end up broken. Pause OneDrive syncing while you work, or keep the project in a folder outside OneDrive (for example C:\Users\<you>\agents-workshop). See Appendix A for more.




“Advanced Setup.” n.d. Accessed September 23, 2026. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup.
Then set up the records. With git:
Set this folder up as a project I'll come back to.

1. Make it a git repository. Before committing anything, add a
   .gitignore that lists snapshots/ and anything else that shouldn't
   be recorded (large data, anything private, system files like
   .DS_Store). Then show me the list of files you would commit, and
   wait for my OK. If git asks for a name and email, ask me what to
   use.
2. Create adr/ with a README.md index and a template.md: title, status
   (accepted, or superseded by ADR-NNNN), date, Context, Decision
   (written with "must" and "must not"), Consequences.
3. If there's no LEDGER.md, create one with the fields Asked, Agent
   did, Checked how, Confidently wrong, Keep.
4. Add to AGENTS.md (create it if needed): read adr/ before changing
   how the app behaves; never edit an accepted ADR to reverse it,
   write a new one that supersedes it; every change gets a ledger
   entry and a commit. If there's no CLAUDE.md, create one containing
   the single line @AGENTS.md.
5. Commit everything as the starting point, then show me the history.
Without git, replace steps 1 and 5 with:
Instead of git, keep snapshots. A snapshot means: copy everything in
this folder except snapshots/ into snapshots/<name>/. Make one before
any change, named for the change. Make the first one now, called
"start", and add the snapshot rule to AGENTS.md.
Check that adr/, LEDGER.md, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md exist, and open AGENTS.md to read the rules the agent wrote for itself. Are they what you asked for? (CLAUDE.md holds only @AGENTS.md, so Claude Code reads the same rules as other agents; Chapter 3 explains why.)


7.4.2 2. Two changes, the full loop
Pick two improvements to your app. Try to make one of them a real decision: something with more than one sensible answer, where you’d want to remember why you chose. Examples: what to do with missing values, which file formats to accept, whether a threshold is fixed or adjustable, whether to use a library. The other can be small.
For each, paste this, with your change filled in:
Next change: <describe it>.

1. If this involves a decision that would be awkward to reverse, write
   an ADR in adr/ first, and show it to me before building.
2. Make the change.
3. Check it: run the tests if there are any, and tell me exactly what
   I should check by hand.
4. Add a ledger entry. "Checked how" says only what was actually run
   or looked at.
5. Show me what's changed since the last commit, then commit it with a
   message that says what changed and why. Show me the history.
(Without git: ask for a snapshot before step 2, and leave out step 5.)
Do the hand check yourself before you let it commit. If the agent’s ADR doesn’t match what you’d decide, say so: the ADR records your decision, not the agent’s suggestion.


7.4.3 3. Break something, then go back
Now make a mistake on purpose, so you’ve seen the way back work before you need it. Choose something whose effect you’ll notice: a label, a calculation, a colour.
For practice: make a deliberate mistake in the app (for example,
<an idea>), and commit it with the message "Deliberate mistake, for
practice". Then show me the history.
Open the app and see the mistake. Then:
Revert the last commit, so the history keeps both the mistake and the
undo. Show me the history, and check that the app is back to how it
was. Then write one ledger entry covering both: what broke, how we
went back, and how we checked.
Without git:
For practice: copy everything in this folder except snapshots/ into
snapshots/before-mistake/. Then make a deliberate mistake
(for example, <an idea>). When I've seen it, restore the app from that
snapshot. Don't touch LEDGER.md or snapshots/ when restoring. Then
write one ledger entry covering both.






TipOptional: a branch for an experiment



With git, try an idea you’re unsure of on a branch: “Make a branch called try-dark-mode, and make the change there” (named for your idea). Look at it. Then say either “merge it into main” or “switch back to main and delete the branch”. Either way, main never saw the half-done version.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.5 What to notice

The agent is good at git, and fast. It knows the commands better than most people. That’s exactly why you ask it to show you what it’s about to commit: speed isn’t the same as checking.
Commit messages are for later readers, including agents. “Update files” is useless in a month. “Reject negative widths, per ADR-0002” tells the next reader, and the next agent session, what happened and why.
Did the agent treat your ADR as a rule? Try asking for a change that contradicts one. Does it stop and point to the record, or cheerfully go ahead? If it goes ahead, look at how the Decision is worded, and at whether AGENTS.md tells it to read adr/.
Going back felt like nothing. That’s the point. Once going back is cheap, you can let the agent try bolder changes.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.6 Check yourself






TipYou’re done when




The history (“show me the history”) has at least four commits: the starting point, two changes and the revert, each with a message that says why. Or, without git, snapshots/ has at least three folders, each named for a change.
adr/ has at least one record, in your words, with a Decision that uses must or must not.
LEDGER.md has an entry for each change, and every “Checked how” names something that was actually run or looked at.
You went back once, and the app works again.
In a new session, “Why does this app …?”, asked about the thing your ADR decided, gets an answer from the ADR.

title: 7  Work like a project
text:
7.7 Going further

GitHub. Putting the folder on GitHub adds a copy off your laptop, issues to track what’s next, pull requests so someone (or another agent) reviews a change before it lands, and automatic tests on every change. It’s also where the privacy warning above starts to matter. PeakPeek’s issue #1 sets out how to build and run it that way, step by step.
Learning git properly. For R users, Happy Git and GitHub for the useR is the kindest introduction. The free Pro Git book is the reference.
More on decision records: the templates and tools collected at adr.github.io, and this workshop’s own adr/ and LEDGER.md.

title: Appendix A — Windows notes

A.1 Documents, and a folder’s full path
Everything in this book works on Windows 10 (version 1809 or later) and Windows 11. Most of it works exactly as on a Mac, because you’re typing plain-English prompts and the agent deals with the operating system. This appendix collects the few places where Windows differs, so chapters can point here instead of repeating themselves.
Your Documents folder is in File Explorer’s left-hand pane, under This PC or your name. On many institution-managed laptops, OneDrive has taken it over, so the real location is:
Either is fine for this book. To see which you have, open the folder in File Explorer and click once in the address bar at the top: it switches from a breadcrumb trail to the full path, which you can copy. You can also right-click a file or folder while holding Shift and choose Copy as path.
The simplest check is the one from Setup: ask the agent “What folder are you in?” It will print the full path.
In PowerShell, this goes to your workshop folder wherever Documents is, OneDrive or not:

A.2 File name extensions and hidden files
By default, File Explorer hides the end of file names, so index.html shows as just index, and SKILL.md as SKILL. This book talks about files by their full names, so turn extensions on:

Windows 11: in File Explorer, View → Show → File name extensions.
Windows 10: in File Explorer, the View tab, then tick File name extensions.

In the same menu, Hidden items shows files and folders whose names start with a dot, such as .claude, where Claude Code keeps skills and settings for a project (Chapter 4). Turn it on too.






WarningA file called notes.txt.txt



With extensions hidden, a file you save as notes.txt from Notepad can end up as notes.txt.txt, and a file the agent made called AGENTS.md looks like a file called AGENTS. If a file “isn’t there” when the agent says it is, turn extensions on first.

You only need a terminal if you use the claude command rather than the desktop app. Windows has two, and they take different commands. Use PowerShell for every command in this book: the installer, cd, claude, claude mcp add in Chapter 5, and winget. Commands shown in grey boxes for Windows are PowerShell commands.

section: A.4 Opening a web page the agent made
text:
A.4 Opening a web page the agent made
Several chapters end with an .html file: a small web page or app that runs entirely in your browser. To open one, double-click it in File Explorer. It opens in your default browser, usually Edge on Windows.
To choose the browser, right-click the file and pick Open with, then Chrome or Edge. Both are fine. The PeakPeek example in Chapter 6 was tested in Chrome.
The address bar will show something like file:///C:/Users/you/Documents/.... That’s expected: the page is reading from your disk, not the internet.

title: Appendix A — Windows notes
text:
A.5 Git for Windows (optional)
Nothing before Chapter 7 needs git. That chapter uses it for version control, and offers a way round if you can’t install it.
Having Git for Windows installed also changes one thing about Claude Code: with it, the agent runs commands through Git Bash (the same kind of shell as on a Mac); without it, the agent uses PowerShell. Either works for this book, and you won’t need to learn Git Bash yourself.
To install it, either download the installer from git-scm.com/install/windows and accept the defaults on every screen, or, in PowerShell:
winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget
Then close and reopen the desktop app or PowerShell, so it finds git.
Or let the agent do it:
Check whether git is installed. If not, tell me how to install Git for Windows
on this computer, and wait for me to say go before running anything.
On an institution-managed laptop, installing software may be blocked. That’s fine: skip it, and use the no-git route in Chapter 7.






WarningGit and OneDrive don’t mix well



OneDrive syncs files while git is writing them, and the two can clash, leaving a project’s history damaged. If your Documents is in OneDrive, either pause OneDrive syncing while you work (from the OneDrive icon in the taskbar), or keep the project in a folder outside OneDrive, such as C:\Users\<you>\agents-workshop, as Chapter 7 suggests.




Line endings. Windows and Macs end lines in text files differently, and Git sometimes prints warnings about LF and CRLF. You can ignore them for everything in this book.

section: A.6 If something else goes wrong
text:
A.6 If something else goes wrong
